To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) short-term C stores supply most of the carbon used for growth, and (2) short-term N stores supply most of nitrogen, but the relative contribution of mobilized stores to leaf growth is regulated by the rate of nitrogen uptake and hence by the C-to-N balance of the substrate supplying the growth process

(1) leaf growth in plants of a grass species is largely dependent on photoassimilate delivered either directly after photosynthesis or after short-term storage; (2) the contribution of mobilized long- and short-term N stores to the N supply of leaf growth is strongly correlated with N uptake; (3) the C:N ratio of substrates used to support leaf growth is determined by both C assimilation and the contribution of mobilization to the supply of N; (4) the relative

(1) leaf growth relies mainly on photoassimilated C, (2) leaf growth depends on N mobilized from short- and long-term stores, and (3) the importance of N mobilized from long-term stores is regulated by internal regulation of N acquisition
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of internal C and N stores in leaf growth and how it relates to plant acclimation to contrasting environmental conditions.
the sources of C and N supplying growth and the role of mobilization from internal stores.
the sources of C and N used to support leaf growth and the role of internal stores.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the role of stores is not determined by C or N acquisition rates but by the balance of current uptake and the rate of N turnover in long-term stores.
the role of stores in supplying C and N for leaf growth is highly dependent on the C-to-N ratios of growth substrates, and that the latter is mainly determined by N uptake rates.
mobilization from stores is of minor importance in C supply to leaf growth, whereas it is a key factor in N supply to leaf growth.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the relative contribution of mobilization from stores is a function of the balance between C and N acquisition and internal regulation of N assimilation.
the role of mobilization from C and N stores as sources of substrates for leaf growth is determined by the relative importance of C and N uptake and the C-to-N ratios of the resulting substrates.
, in the C and N economy of leaf growth, short-term storage plays a key role in the C supply, and long-term storage in the N supply.
The main takeaway from our work is that
mobilization from stores is an important component of leaf growth in plants, especially when growth is limited.
the relative importance of stores as a source for growth is not determined by the C acquisition rate of plants, but is rather a function of their N uptake rate.
the role of stores in supplying growth substrates is highly dynamic and can be modulated by environmental and plant factors.
